title: Design Patterns
description: Common design patterns in software development

categories.name: Creational Patterns
categories.description: Patterns that deal with object creation mechanisms

patterns.name: Singleton
patterns.description: Ensures a class has only one instance and provides a global point of access to it.
patterns.analogy: Like having one president for a country at any given time.
use_cases: For shared resources (database connections, thread pools)
when_to_use: When you need exactly one instance of a class
When the instance should be accessible globally
For shared resources with controlled access

implementations.title: Traditional Java way (Thread-safe with double-checked locking)
In Spring, it's much simpler

considerations: Singleton scope management in Spring context
patterns.spring_usage: In Spring, every bean is a singleton by default!
patterns.how_it_works: Spring manages the entire lifecycle, ensuring only one instance exists without you writing a single line of singleton code.

patterns.name: Factory Method
patterns.description: Defines an interface for creating an object, but lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate.
patterns.analogy: Like a restaurant where you order a meal (the interface), but the chef decides how to prepare it (the implementation).
use_cases: When a class can't anticipate which objects it must create
When you want to delegate responsibility to subclasses
when_to_use: When a class can't anticipate which objects it must create
When you want to delegate responsibility to subclasses
When you need to work with objects through a common interface

implementations.title: Basic Factory Method Pattern
Spring Example

patterns.spring_usage: Spring's BeanFactory is a sophisticated implementation of this pattern.
patterns.how_it_works: Spring creates objects with the right dependencies automatically, handling all the complexity of instantiation.

patterns.name: Abstract Factory
patterns.description: Provides an interface for creating families of related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes.
patterns.analogy: Like a furniture factory that can produce chairs, tables, and sofas in various styles (modern, Victorian, etc.).
use_cases: When system must be independent of how products are created
When families of related products are designed to be used together
when_to_use: When the system needs to be independent of how its products are created
When you need to ensure that libraries work with families of related objects
When you want to provide a class library of products and reveal just their interfaces

implementations.title: Abstract Factory Implementation
Spring Example

patterns.spring_usage: Spring's ApplicationContext implementing different context types

patterns.name: Builder
patterns.description: Separates the construction of a complex object from its representation.
patterns.analogy: Like a sandwich shop where you specify each ingredient step by step until your custom sandwich is complete.
use_cases: When you need to create complex objects with many optional parameters
when_to_use: When you need to create complex objects with many optional parameters
To avoid telescoping constructors (constructors with many parameters)
To create immutable objects
When construction involves multiple steps

implementations.title: Builder Implementation
User Object with Builder

patterns.how_it_works: Construct complex objects step by step with fluent interfaces, making complex creation feel elegant.

patterns.name: Prototype
patterns.description: Creates new objects by cloning an existing instance.
patterns.analogy: Like a blueprint that can be duplicated to create identical objects quickly.
use_cases: When system should be independent of how products are created
When instances of a class can have one of only a few different combinations of state
when_to_use: When object creation is expensive
When instances of a class can have limited combinations of state
When you need to avoid building a class hierarchy of factories
When classes to instantiate are specified at run-time

implementations.title: Basic Prototype Pattern
Spring Prototype Scope

categories.name: Structural Patterns
categories.description: Patterns that deal with object composition and relationships

patterns.name: Adapter
patterns.description: Allows incompatible interfaces to work together by wrapping an instance of one class with a new adapter class.
patterns.analogy: Like a power adapter that allows a US plug to work in a European socket.
use_cases: When you need to integrate with a legacy system or third-party library
When you want to reuse existing classes that don't have the interface you need
when_to_use: When you need to use an existing class with an incompatible interface
When you want to create a reusable class that cooperates with classes that don't have compatible interfaces
When you need to use several existing subclasses but it's impractical to adapt their interface

implementations.title: Basic Adapter Pattern
Legacy User System Adapter in Spring

patterns.name: Bridge
patterns.description: Separates abstraction from implementation so they can vary independently.
patterns.analogy: Like remote controls (abstraction) working with different devices (implementation).
use_cases: When you want to avoid permanent binding between abstraction and implementation
When both abstraction and implementation should be extensible through subclasses
when_to_use: When you want to avoid a permanent binding between an abstraction and its implementation
When both the abstractions and their implementations should be extensible independently
When changes in the implementation should not impact the client code
When you have a proliferation of classes resulting from a coupled interface and numerous implementations

implementations.title: Basic Bridge Pattern
Spring Example with Messaging

patterns.name: Composite
patterns.description: Composes objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies.
patterns.analogy: Like an organizational chart where both individual employees and departments are treated uniformly.
use_cases: When clients need to ignore difference between compositions of objects and individual objects
When object structure can have nested compositions
when_to_use: When you want to represent part-whole hierarchies of objects
When you want clients to be able to ignore the difference between compositions of objects and individual objects
When the structure can have nested compositions
When you want the client code to work with all objects in the hierarchy uniformly

implementations.title: Basic Composite Pattern
Spring Security Example

patterns.name: Decorator
patterns.description: Attaches additional responsibilities to objects dynamically without modifying their structure.
patterns.analogy: Like adding toppings to an ice cream cone - the core is still ice cream, but you've enhanced it.
use_cases: When you need to add functionality to objects without changing their underlying code
When extension by subclassing is impractical
when_to_use: When you need to add functionality to objects without changing their underlying code
When extension by subclassing is impractical or leads to excessive subclasses
When you need to dynamically add or remove object behaviors
When you want to add responsibilities to individual objects without affecting others

implementations.title: Basic Decorator Pattern
Data Source Example

patterns.how_it_works: Stack capabilities by composing objects rather than inheritance, creating flexible, modular code.

patterns.name: Facade
patterns.description: Provides a unified interface to a set of interfaces in a subsystem.
patterns.analogy: Like a customer service department that handles all customer inquiries without exposing internal departments.
use_cases: When you need to provide a simple interface to a complex subsystem
When there are many dependencies between clients and implementation classes
when_to_use: When you need to provide a simple interface to a complex subsystem
When you want to layer your subsystems
When you want to decouple your subsystem from clients and other subsystems
When you need to structure a subsystem into layers

implementations.title: Basic Facade Pattern
Spring Boot Service Facade

patterns.how_it_works: The template handles all the boilerplate while you focus on the unique parts, creating cleaner, more focused code.

patterns.name: Flyweight
patterns.description: Uses sharing to support large numbers of fine-grained objects efficiently.
patterns.analogy: Like a character library in a word processor where each character is only stored once but displayed multiple times.
use_cases: When an application uses a large number of objects that have some shared state
When the application needs many objects that would use too much memory
when_to_use: When an application uses a large number of objects
When storage costs are high because of the quantity of objects
When most object state can be made extrinsic
When many objects can be replaced by a few shared objects

implementations.title: Basic Flyweight Pattern
Spring Cache Implementation

patterns.name: Proxy
patterns.description: Provides a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access to it.
patterns.analogy: Like a bouncer at a club who controls who gets access to the club.
use_cases: For lazy loading of expensive resources
For logging requests or adding authentication
when_to_use: For lazy loading of expensive resources
For access control to the original object
For logging requests or adding authentication
For implementing remote access
When you need a more versatile or sophisticated reference to an object than a simple pointer

implementations.title: Basic Proxy Pattern
Spring AOP Example

patterns.spring_usage: Spring AOP and @Transactional use proxies under the hood.
patterns.how_it_works: Spring dynamically creates proxy objects that add behavior (like transaction management) without modifying your original code.

categories.name: Behavioral Patterns
categories.description: Patterns that deal with communication between objects

patterns.name: Observer
patterns.description: Defines a one-to-many dependency between objects so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified.
patterns.analogy: Like subscribers to a YouTube channel who get notified when a new video is uploaded.
use_cases: When a change to one object requires changing others, and you don't know how many objects need to change
When an object should be able to notify other objects without knowing who they are
when_to_use: When a change to one object requires changing others, and you don't know how many objects need to change
When an object should be able to notify other objects without knowing who they are
When you need to respect the principle of loose coupling
When you want a publish-subscribe interaction model

implementations.title: Basic Observer Pattern
Spring Event Example

patterns.spring_usage: Spring's event mechanism is an implementation of the observer pattern.
patterns.how_it_works: Components can react to events without direct coupling to the source, creating a beautifully decoupled system.

patterns.name: Strategy
patterns.description: Defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable.
patterns.analogy: Like choosing a transportation method (car, bike, bus) based on weather, distance, or time constraints.
use_cases: When you want to define a class that will have one behavior that is similar to other behaviors in a list
When you need to use different variants of an algorithm within an object
when_to_use: When you want to define a class that will have one behavior that is similar to other behaviors in a list
When you need to use different variants of an algorithm within an object
When an algorithm uses data that clients shouldn't know about
When a class defines many behaviors as conditional statements

implementations.title: Basic Strategy Pattern
Payment Strategy Example

patterns.how_it_works: You can swap strategies without changing the client code, creating adaptable, flexible systems.

patterns.name: Template Method
patterns.description: Defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a method, deferring some steps to subclasses.
patterns.analogy: Like a recipe that outlines the general steps (mix, bake, cool) but leaves specific ingredients to variations.
use_cases: When you want to let clients extend only particular steps of an algorithm, but not the whole algorithm
When you have several classes that contain almost identical algorithms with some minor differences
when_to_use: When you want to let clients extend only particular steps of an algorithm, but not the whole algorithm
When you have several classes that contain almost identical algorithms with some minor differences
When you want to control subclasses extensions
When you want to avoid code duplication by factoring common behavior into a single class

implementations.title: Basic Template Method Pattern
Document Processor Example

patterns.spring_usage: Spring's JdbcTemplate is a great example of this pattern.
patterns.how_it_works: The template handles all the boilerplate while you focus on the unique parts, creating cleaner, more focused code.

patterns.name: State
patterns.description: Allows object to alter behavior when internal state changes.
patterns.analogy: Like a traffic light that changes its behavior based on its current state (red, yellow, green).
use_cases: When an object's behavior depends on its state
When operations have large conditional statements that depend on the object's state
when_to_use: When an object's behavior depends on its state, and it must change its behavior at runtime depending on that state
When operations have large, multipart conditional statements that depend on the object's state
When you want to avoid exposing state-specific behaviors across multiple classes
When state transitions are explicit

implementations.title: Basic State Pattern
Order Processing State Example

patterns.name: Visitor
patterns.description: Represents an operation to be performed on elements of an object structure.
patterns.analogy: Like a tour guide who knows how to navigate through different parts of a museum.
use_cases: When you need to perform operations across a disparate object structure
When you want to add new operations without changing classes of the elements on which it operates
when_to_use: When you need to perform operations across a disparate object structure
When many distinct and unrelated operations need to be performed on objects in an object structure
When the object structure classes rarely change, but you often want to define new operations over the structure
When you want to avoid polluting the object structure classes with various operation methods

implementations.title: Basic Visitor Pattern
Document Visitor Example

patterns.description: Defines an object that encapsulates how a set of objects interact

implementation_tips: Start simple - Don't over-engineer; use patterns only when they add value
Understand the problem first - Choose a pattern based on the problem, not the other way around
Combine patterns - Real-world solutions often involve multiple patterns
Consider Spring's built-in implementations - Spring already implements many patterns for you
Document your use of patterns - Help other developers understand your design decisions
patterns_in_spring_boot: Dependency Injection - The core of Spring is based on the Dependency Inversion Principle
Factory Pattern - Spring's BeanFactory creates objects
Singleton Pattern - Beans are singletons by default
Proxy Pattern - Used for AOP and transaction management
Template Method Pattern - JdbcTemplate, RestTemplate, etc.
